title: Learning disability | NHS inform
text:
Learning disability
A learning disability is a significant life-long condition which affects development. If you have a learning disability you may need help to:
understand information
learn new skills
cope independently
A learning disability is different for everyone. No two people are the same.
People usually have a learning disability from birth or early childhood. People with a learning disability can learn and develop with the right support and opportunities.
Sometimes a learning disability is called an intellectual disability.
What is the difference between a learning disability and a learning difficulty?
A learning disability affects all parts of daily life. For example, social, emotional, practical and educational skills.
A learning difficulty is a condition that makes learning a specific skill harder. For example, dyslexia (reading), dyspraxia (coordination), and dyscalculia (number). Sometimes this is called a specific learning difficulty.
A person can have both a learning disability and a specific learning difficulty.
Learning disability and Down’s syndrome
Down’s syndrome
is a genetic condition. Everyone with Down’s syndrome has some level of learning disability.
Learning disability and autism
Around a third of people
with a learning disability are also autistic.
Read more about autism
What causes a learning disability?
The cause of a learning disability isn’t always known.
A learning disability can develop at different stages.
This can happen before birth, for example:
if you have a genetic condition like
Down’s syndrome
, Fragile X syndrome or
Edward’s syndrome
infections during pregnancy
exposure to toxins like alcohol or drugs during pregnancy
During birth, for example:
premature birth
lack of oxygen
birth trauma
After birth, for example:
infections like
meningitis
accidents or head injuries
seizures or early childhood illnesses
exposure to toxins like alcohol or drugs
Diagnosing a learning disability
A learning disability can be diagnosed at any time.
Diagnosed is when you’re told you have a condition or illness by a doctor or another health professional.
A child may be diagnosed at birth or during early childhood. For some people it may be many years before they receive a diagnosis. Some people may never receive a diagnosis at all.
Although getting a diagnosis can be a very difficult and emotional experience, it can help to access the care and support needed for the future.
Speak to your GP practice if you think you or a loved one has a learning disability.
Living with a learning disability
With the right support, people with a learning disability can lead happy and full lives.
The amount of support you’ll be offered depends on your needs.
Some people with a learning disability may only need a bit of support with specific tasks like getting the bus or household tasks.
Some people are likely to need more care and support with many things they do.
Learning disability and health
Someone with a learning disability can have the same health conditions as anyone else.
There are some conditions which people with a learning disability are more likely to have. This can include:
respiratory problems like
pneumonia
and
acute respiratory infections
some types of
cancer
diabetes
epilepsy
constipation
mental health conditions
sensory and hearing impairments
gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
(
GORD
)
dyspepsia
dementia
Sometimes people with a learning disability don’t get the help they need with health conditions and illnesses. Communication and sensory differences can make it difficult for a person with a learning disability to recognise and explain their symptoms.
People with a learning disability are entitled to the same healthcare services as everyone else. This includes
dental care
,
health screening
, and
mental health support
.
Annual health check
If you have a learning disability you’re entitled to an annual health check every year from the age of 16.
Read more about
annual health checks for people with a learning disability
.
Learning disability services
Learning disability services are tailored to the needs of people with a learning disability.
Learning disability services provide:
specialist healthcare
treatment
support for families and carers
help for other health and social care teams
Support can vary depending on where you live. Speak to your GP practice to find out what’s available in your area. You could also check your local health board’s website to find out about local learning disability services in your area.
Some learning disability services work with children and adults, and some only work with adults.
Learning disability nurses
Learning disability nurses can support people with a learning disability from birth to end of life care. They also support families and carers of people with a learning disability.
Learning disability nurses work across all settings, for example in:
hospitals
communities
schools
social care
There are learning disability nurses in each local health board. Contact your local learning disability nursing team for more information.
They work as part of a team, for example with:
social workers
psychiatrists
occupational therapists
speech and language therapists
psychologists
Getting support for a child or young person with a learning disability
Health, education and social care services should work together with you and your child to find out what support they need. Support can vary depending on where you live.
They should then put a plan in place for them. This is called a co-ordinated support plan. This plan should support children until they transition to adult services.
If you’re a parent or carer of a child or young person with a learning disability and you’re worried about their health, speak to their:
GP practice
health visitor
school nurse
Getting support for an adult with a learning disability
Your local council’s social care team should work with you to find out what support you need. This is called a needs assessment. Support can vary depending on where you live.
Your family, carer or support worker can help you with this if you need them to.
How to get an assessment of your care needs
Self Directed Support (SDS) Scotland
also have information about assessment of needs
.
If you’re the family member, partner or friend of someone who needs ongoing care or support you can
read about working and supporting someone’s health or care on gov.uk
.
Advocacy support
Everyone has the right to get support from another person to help express their views and wishes (for example, at a healthcare appointment). This person is called an advocate.
Advocates can be helpful if you:
find it difficult to communicate your views
need other people to listen to you and take your views into account
Read more about advocacy
